claim: G4s are built by stacked guanine tetrads connected via Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds and can be formed by intra- or inter-molecular folding of the tetramers.
source: G4s are built by stacked guanine tetrads connected via Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds and can be formed by intra- or inter-molecular folding of the tetramers (Panyutin et al., 1989; Sen and Gilbert, 1988; Sundquist and Klug, 1989; Williamson et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Panyutin et al., 1989; Sen and Gilbert, 1988; Sundquist and Klug, 1989; Williamson et al., 1989).

claim: R-loops are three-stranded structures containing a DNA-RNA hybrid and a displaced single-stranded DNA.
source: R-loops are three-stranded structures containing a DNA-RNA hybrid and a displaced single-stranded DNA (Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012; Xu and Clayton, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012; Xu and Clayton, 1996).

claim: Both G4s and R-loops are involved in key biological processes, including transcription, replication, genomic instability, class switch recombination in B cells, DNA damage and repair, and telomere maintenance.
source: Both G4s and R-loops are involved in key biological processes, including transcription, replication, genomic instability, class switch recombination in B cells, DNA damage and repair, and telomere maintenance (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2017; Varshney et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2017; Varshney et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023).

claim: R-loops appear to have a strong sequence preference with high G/C ratios.
source: R-loops appear to have a strong sequence preference with high G/C ratios (Ginno et al., 2013; Ginno et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ginno et al., 2013; Ginno et al., 2012).

claim: Specific G4 ligands stabilized G4s and simultaneously increase R-loop levels within minutes in human cancer cells, which finally induced DNA damage.
source: Specific G4 ligands stabilized G4s and simultaneously increase R-loop levels within minutes in human cancer cells, which finally induced DNA damage (De Magis et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (De Magis et al., 2019).

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been reported to induce G4 and R-loop formation at transcriptionally active sites, and their inter-regulation is essential for the DNA repair.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) have been reported to induce G4 and R-loop formation at transcriptionally active sites, and their inter-regulation is essential for the DNA repair (Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Tan et al., 2020).

claim: In a reconstituted eukaryotic DNA replication system, the interplay of R-loops and G4s was shown to impact replication fork progression by inducing fork stalling.
source: In a reconstituted eukaryotic DNA replication system, the interplay of R-loops and G4s was shown to impact replication fork progression by inducing fork stalling (Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Kumar et al., 2021).

claim: Single-molecule fluorescence studies showed the existence of a positive feedback mechanism of G4 and R-loop formation during transcription, where the transcription-induced R-loop precedes and facilitates G4 formation in the non-template strand, and in turn, G4 promotes the R-loop formation in the following rounds of transcription.
source: Single-molecule fluorescence studies showed the existence of a positive feedback mechanism of G4 and R-loop formation during transcription, where the transcription-induced R-loop precedes and facilitates G4 formation in the non-template strand, and in turn, G4 promotes the R-loop formation in the following rounds of transcription (Lee et al., 2020; Lim and Hohng, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Lee et al., 2020; Lim and Hohng, 2020).

claim: CTCF-bound sites are enriched for R-loops and G4s which facilitate CTCF binding to promote chromatin looping interactions.
source: Wulfridge et al. reported that the architectural protein CCCTC binding factor (CTCF)-bound sites are enriched for R-loops and G4s which facilitate CTCF binding to promote chromatin looping interactions (Wulfridge et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Wulfridge et al., 2023).

claim: A group of helicases, RNA-binding factors, endonucleases, and DNA topoisomerases cooperate to actively dissolve G4s and R-loops restoring B-formed DNA duplexes.
source: given that a group of helicases, RNA-binding factors, endonucleases, and DNA topoisomerases cooperate to actively dissolve G4s and R-loops restoring B-formed DNA duplexes (Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2017; Varshney et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hänsel-Hertsch et al., 2017; Varshney et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023).

claim: A steady state equilibrium of G4s and R-loops is generally set at low levels in living cells under physiological conditions.
source: a steady state equilibrium is generally set at low levels in living cells under physiological conditions (Miglietta et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Miglietta et al., 2020).

claim: The specificity of the S9.6 antibody on R-loops has been questioned recently for accurate quantification and mapping of R-loops.
source: Additionally, the specificity of the S9.6 antibody on R-loops has been questioned recently for accurate quantification and mapping of R-loops (Hartono et al., 2018; König et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hartono et al., 2018; König et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2013).

claim: G4s could tightly form a complex with the cellular cofactor hemin both in vitro and in living cells, where hemin binds by end-stacking on the terminal G-quartets of G4s without affecting the folding of G4s.
source: Recent studies showed that G4s could tightly form a complex with the cellular cofactor hemin both in vitro and in living cells, where hemin binds by end-stacking on the terminal G-quartets of G4s without affecting the folding of G4s (Gray et al., 2019; Stadlbauer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Gray et al., 2019; Stadlbauer et al., 2021).

claim: The G4-hemin complex has been shown to act as a peroxidase to catalyze oxidation reactions in the presence of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
source: The G4-hemin complex has been shown to act as a peroxidase to catalyze oxidation reactions in the presence of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (Cheng et al., 2009; Lat et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Cheng et al., 2009; Lat et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2011).

claim: The H2O2-activated G4-hemin complex oxidizes the biotin tyramide to phenoxyl radicals that covalently conjugate biotin to G4 itself and its proximal DNA within 10 nm (equivalent to approximately 31 bp) in vitro and in vivo.
source: The H2O2-activated G4-hemin complex oxidizes the biotin tyramide to phenoxyl redicals that covalently conjugate biotin to G4 itself and its proximal DNA within 10 nm (equivalent to approximately 31 bp) in vitro and in vivo (Einarson and Sen, 2017; Lat et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Einarson and Sen, 2017; Lat et al., 2020).

claim: The HBD domain of RNase H1 mediates the specific recognition of DNA/RNA hybrid in a sequence-independent manner, which is a gold standard for R-loop recognition in the cell.
source: The HBD domain of RNase H1 mediates the specific recognition of DNA/RNA hybrid in a sequence-independent manner, which is a gold standard for R-loop recognition in the cell (Nowotny et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Nowotny et al., 2008).

claim: The catalytically inactive RNase H1 or its HBD domain-based methods have been successfully used to identify genome-wide native R-loops.
source: The catalytically inactive RNase H1 or its HBD domain -based methods have been successfully used to identify genome-wide native R-loops (Chen et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: The free heme concentration in normal human erythrocytes is 21±2 µM.
source: The free heme concentration in normal human erythrocytes is 21±2 µM (Aich et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Aich et al., 2015).

claim: HEK293 cells treated with hemin and Bio-An exhibited a robust fluorescence signal, while the absence of either hemin or Bio-An almost completely abolished the biotinylation signals.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, cells treated with hemin and Bio-An exhibited a robust fluorescence signal, while the absence of either hemin or Bio-An almost completely abolished the biotinylation signals, suggesting a specific and active biotinylation activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating fluorescence signals under different treatment conditions.

claim: The hemin treatment condition used does not significantly affect G4 folding.
source: These data suggest that the hemin treatment condition we used does not significantly affect G4 folding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar BG4 CUT&Tag signals between hemin-treated and control samples, with only 174 peaks showing differential signals.

claim: Hemin-induced proximal biotinylation of G4s could be utilized to mark the native G4s in living cells.
source: Therefore, hemin-induced proximal biotinylation of G4s could be utilized to mark the native G4s in living cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing specific biotinylation and minimal effect on G4 folding.

claim: HepG4-seq identified 6,799 consensus peaks from two independent biological repeats in HEK293 cells.
source: Deep sequencing analysis of the biotinylated G4s fragments identified 6,799 consensus peaks from two independent biological repeats in HEK293 cells
evidence: Supported by experimental data from HepG4-seq analysis.

claim: G4s are mainly localized in promoters (38.7%) and gene bodies (47.1%).
source: Genomic distribution analysis showed that G4s are mainly localized in promoters (38.7%) and gene bodies (47.1%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The peaks identified by HepG4-seq overlap quite well with the center of pqsfinder max Scores that report the PQS quality.
source: The peaks identified by HepG4-seq overlap quite well with the center of pqsfinder max Scores that report the PQS quality (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: G-rich sequences are highly prevalent in HepG4-seq peaks.
source: The motif enrichment analysis by HOMER (Heinz et al., 2010) revealed a high prevalence of G-rich sequences in HepG4-seq peaks (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The RecQ-like helicases Bloom syndrome protein (BLM) and Werner syndrome ATP-dependent helicase (WRN) are the first recognized and the best-characterized DNA G4-resolving mammalian helicases.
source: The RecQ-like helicases Bloom syndrome protein (BLM) and Werner syndrome ATP-dependent helicase (WRN) are the first recognized and the best-characterized DNA G4-resolving mammalian helicases (Fry and Loeb, 1999; Mendoza et al., 2016; Mohaghegh et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Fry and Loeb, 1999; Mendoza et al., 2016; Mohaghegh et al., 2001).

claim: ML216 and NSC617145 are selective and cell-permeable inhibitors of BLM and WRN, respectively, by inhibiting their ATPase activity.
source: The small molecules ML216 and NSC617145 are selective and cell-permeable inhibitors of BLM and WRN, respectively, by inhibiting their ATPase activity (Aggarwal et al., 2013a; Aggarwal et al., 2013b; Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Aggarwal et al., 2013a; Aggarwal et al., 2013b; Nguyen et al., 2013).

claim: Treatment of ML216 or NSC617145 remarkably elevated signals of native G4s.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of the treated cells using Strep-647 showed that the treatment of ML216 or NSC617145 remarkably elevated signals of native G4s (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: HepG4-seq identified 77,003 peaks from ML216- or NSC617145-treated HEK293 cells.
source: Notably, HepG4-seq identified 77,003 peaks from ML216- or NSC617145- treated HEK293 cells
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq experimental data.

claim: ~70,000 new G4 peaks were induced by inhibition of BLM or WRN.
source: ~70,000 new G4 peaks were induced by inhibition of BLM or WRN (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq experimental data comparing treated and untreated cells.

claim: The signals of G4s detected by HepG4-seq were significantly increased after inhibiting BLM or WRN.
source: The signals of G4s detected by HepG4-seq were significantly increased after inhibiting BLM or WRN (Figure 1H and I) (Mann-Whitney test, p<2.2E-16).
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: HepG4-seq is able to efficiently detect dynamic native G4s.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that HepG4-seq is able to efficiently detect dynamic native G4s.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing detection of G4s under different conditions.

claim: HBD-seq revealed 42,488 consensus native R-loops peaks with a high signal-to-noise ratio in HEK293 cells.
source: We performed the HBD-seq on HEK293 cells, and revealed 42,488 consensus native R-loops peaks with a high signal-to-noise ratio
evidence: Supported by HBD-seq experimental data.

claim: HBD-seq signals were dramatically diminished in HEK293 cells treated with RNases prior to HBD-seq.
source: while the HBD-seq signals were dramatically diminished in HEK293 cells treated with the RNases prior to HBD-seq (Figure 2B), suggesting the specificity of HBD-seq in detecting native R-loops.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating RNase sensitivity.

claim: 5030 native co-localized peaks were revealed in HEK293 cells, ranging in size from 100 bp to ~1.5 kb.
source: We then analyzed the regions co-occupied by both HepG4-seq-identified G4s and HBD-seq-identified R-loops, and revealed 5030 native co-localized peaks in HEK293 cells, ranging in size from 100 bp to ~1.5 kb (Figure 2C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of HepG4-seq and HBD-seq data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: 73.8% of co-localized peaks are localized at promoters, 5'UTR, exon1, and intron 1.
source: 73.8% of these co-localized peaks are localized at promoters, 5'UTR, exon1, and intron 1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A distinct peak was detected around the transcription start site (TSS) in metagene analysis of co-localized peaks.
source: When we performed a metagene analysis of these co-localized peaks, a distinct peak was detected around the transcription start site (TSS) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by metagene analysis data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: G-rich sequences are highly enriched in the co-localized peaks.
source: The motifs enrichment analysis by HOMER (Heinz et al., 2010) showed that G-rich sequences are highly enriched in the co-localized peaks (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The RNA levels of co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes are significantly higher than all genes, G4s or R-loops-associated genes.
source: RNA-seq analysis revealed that the RNA levels of co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes are significantly higher than all genes, G4s or R-loops- associated genes with the Mann-Whitney test p<2.2E-16 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The co-localized G4s and R-loops are mainly localized within 1 kb of the TSS of transcriptionally active genes (~60% peaks with FPKM ≥ 5).
source: Different from G4s and R-loops, the co-localized G4s and R-loops are mainly localized within 1 kb of the TSS of transcriptionally active genes (~60% peaks with FPKM ≥ 5) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by distribution analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Hundreds of genes were linked to co-localized G4s and R-loops with increased G4 signals and exhibited significant changes in expression levels upon inhibition of BLM or WRN in HEK293 cells.
source: As a result, hundreds of genes were linked to co-localized G4s and R-loops with increased G4 signals (at least 1.5 foldchange) and at the same time exhibited significant changes in expression levels upon inhibition of BLM or WRN in HEK293 cells (Figure 3C), suggesting that co-localized G4s and R-loops could regulate the transcription of their associated genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and HepG4-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 125 genes were co-regulated by both ML216 and NSC617145.
source: Among the differential genes, 125 genes were co-regulated by both ML216 and NSC617145 (Figure 3E), suggesting that BLM and WRN could co-regulate the transcription of genes by resolving G4s.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Co-localized G4s & R-loops-regulated genes in HEK293 cells are mainly involved in cell cycle regulation, DNA/mRNA metabolic regulation, DNA damage response, chromatin binding, kinase binding, cell-substrate junction, et al.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed that co-localized G4s & R-loops-regulated genes in HEK293 cells are mainly involved in cell cycle regulation, DNA/mRNA metabolic regulation, DNA damage response, chromatin binding, kinase binding, cell-substrate junction, et al (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 68,482 native overlapping peaks were uncovered in mESCs, ranging in size from 100 bp to ~2 kb.
source: To understand the regulatory roles of co-localized G4s and R-loops in mESCs, we performed the HepG4-seq and HBD-seq on mESCs and finally uncovered 68,482 native overlapping peaks in mESCs, ranging in size from 100 bp to ~2 kb (Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq and HBD-seq data in mESCs shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: A large number of native G4s (95,128) were identified by HepG4-seq in mESCs.
source: Notably, unlike HEK293 cells, a large number of native G4s (95,128) were identified by HepG4-seq in mESCs (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq data in mESCs shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Native G4s exhibit obvious cell type-specific distribution.
source: which well overlap with the PQS predicted by pqsfinder (Figure 4B), suggesting that native G4s exhibit obvious cell type-specific distribution.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of G4 numbers between HEK293 cells and mESCs.

claim: Only 34.2% peaks are localized in promoters, exon1, and intron1 while 25.9% peaks in intergenic regions in mESCs.
source: For the genomic distribution of co-localized G4s and R-loops, unlike HEK293 cells, only 34.2% peaks are localized in promoters, exon1, and intron1 while 25.9% peaks in intergenic regions (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The distinct number and localization feature of co-localized G4s and R-loops in HEK293 cells and mESCs shows the cell type-specific distribution.
source: The distinct number and localization feature of co-localized G4s and R-loops in HEK293 cells and mESCs shows the cell type-specific distribution.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of distribution patterns between HEK293 cells and mESCs.

claim: The metagene analysis of overlapping peaks exhibited a distinct peak around TSS.
source: The metagene analysis of overlapping peaks exhibited a distinct peak around TSS (Figure 4F), suggesting the potential for transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Supported by metagene analysis data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: G-rich sequences are highly enriched in overlapping peaks in mESCs, similar to those in HEK293 cells.
source: The motifs enrichment analysis found that G-rich sequences are highly enriched in these overlapping peaks, similar to those in HEK293 cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The RNA levels of co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes were seen to be significantly higher in mESCs.
source: Similar to HEK293 cells, the RNA levels of co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes were seen to be significantly higher in mESCs (Mann-Whitney test p<2.2E-16) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The overlapping peaks in mESCs are mainly localized in the proximal promoters (1 kb from TSS, 9063 peaks with FPKM ≥ 5) and the region 5–50 kb from the TSS of transcriptionally active genes (32,690 peaks with FPKM ≥ 5).
source: However, unlike in HEK293 cells (Figure 3B), the overlapping peaks in mESCs are mainly localized in the proximal promoters (1 kb from TSS, 9063 peaks with FPKM ≥ 5) and the region 5–50 kb from the TSS of transcriptionally active genes (32,690 peaks with FPKM ≥ 5) (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by distribution analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-localized G4s and R-loops are possibly distributed in active promoters or enhancers.
source: suggesting that co-localized G4s and R-loops are possibly distributed in active promoters or enhancers.
evidence: Inferred from the distribution pattern of co-localized peaks relative to TSS and gene expression.

claim: Co-localized G4s and R-loops were observed to well overlap with active chromatin markers (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me1) and RNAP but not the repressed chromatin marker H3K27me3.
source: As a result, co-localized G4s and R-loops were observed to well overlap with active chromatin markers (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me1) and RNAP but not the repressed chromatin marker H3K27me3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by co-localization analysis with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 20,741 and 19,726 co-localized G4s and R-loops are found in promoters and enhancers, respectively.
source: Notably, 20,741 and 19,726 co-localized G4s and R-loops are found in promoters and enhancers, respectively
evidence: Supported by genomic annotation analysis.

claim: 18,496 peaks are seen in active promoters.
source: 18,496 peaks are seen in active promoters
evidence: Supported by genomic annotation analysis.

claim: 15,787 peaks are seen in active enhancers.
source: 15,787 peaks are seen in active enhancers (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in active promoters show high and almost equal signals of G4s and R-loops, and enrich H3K4me3, H3K27ac, and RNAP.
source: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in active promoters show high and almost equal signals of G4s and R-loops, and enrich H3K4me3, H3K27ac, and RNAP (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-localized G4s and R-loops at active promoters are likely linked to promoter-associated nascent RNAs.
source: The co-localization of G4s, R-loops and RNAP at active promoters suggests that co-localized G4s and R-loops are likely linked to promoter-associated nascent RNAs (Core et al., 2008; Li and Fu, 2019; Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization with RNAP and supported by citations to prior work on nascent RNAs (Core et al., 2008; Li and Fu, 2019; Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008).

claim: A medium level of H3K4me1 is present in a bimodal pattern beside co-localized G4s and R-loops at active promoters.
source: Interestingly, a medium level of H3K4me1 is present in a bimodal pattern beside co-localized G4s and R-loops at active promoters (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in bivalent promoters exhibit low signals of both G4s and R-loops, and overlap with a high level of H3K27me3, a medium level of H3K4me1, and a low level of H3K4m3.
source: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in bivalent promoters exhibit low signals of both G4s and R-loops, and overlap with a high level of H3K27me3, a medium level of H3K4me1, and a low level of H3K4m3 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in active enhancers exhibit sharp peaks and well overlap with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and RNAP.
source: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in active enhancers exhibit sharp peaks and well overlap with H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and RNAP
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks.

claim: The co-localized G4s and R-loops in poised enhancers enrich the active histone marks H3K4me1 and H3K4me3, and the repressive mark H3K27me3 while the signal of RNAP is very low.
source: the co-localized G4s and R-loops in poised enhancers enrich the active histone marks H3K4me1 and H3K4me3, and the repressive mark H3K27me3 while the signal of RNAP is very low (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The unmarked enhancers-associated co-localized G4s and R-loops show low levels of all marks tested.
source: The unmarked enhancers-associated co-localized G4s and R-loops show low levels of all marks tested.
evidence: Supported by analysis of chromatin marks.

claim: The co-occupancy of eRNAs are likely involved in the formation of co-localized G4s and R-loops in enhancers.
source: Given that enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) have been widely identified as non-coding RNAs in enhancers and are functionally important for enhancer activity (Andersson et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2010; Sigova et al., 2015), the co-occupacy of eRNAs are likely involved in the formation of co-localized G4s and R-loops in enhancers and shed light on the new regulatory mechanism of eRNA action.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of co-localized G4s and R-loops in enhancers and supported by citations on eRNAs (Andersson et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2010; Sigova et al., 2015).

claim: Dhx9 is a versatile helicase capable of directly resolving R-loops and G4s or promoting R-loop formation by unwinding secondary structures in the nascent RNA strand.
source: Dhx9 (also known as RNA Helicase A) is a versatile helicase capable of directly resolving R-loops and G4s or promoting R-loop formation by unwinding secondary structures in the nascent RNA strand (Chakraborty and Grosse, 2011; Chakraborty et al., 2018; Cristini et al., 2018; Matsui et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Chakraborty and Grosse, 2011; Chakraborty et al., 2018; Cristini et al., 2018; Matsui et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021).

claim: Dhx9 has been reported to play roles in DNA replication, transcription, translation, RNA processing and transport and maintenance of genomic stability.
source: and has been reported to play roles in DNA replication, transcription, translation, RNA processing and transport and maintenance of genomic stability (Aktaş et al., 2017; Aratani et al., 2001; Chellini et al., 2022; Jain et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Aktaş et al., 2017; Aratani et al., 2001; Chellini et al., 2022; Jain et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2022).

claim: Dhx9 is a promising regulator of co-localized G4s and R-loops.
source: Thus, Dhx9 is a promising regulator of co-localized G4s and R-loops.
evidence: Inferred from Dhx9's known capabilities in resolving G4s and R-loops.

claim: A large amount of G4s or R-loops within co-localized G4s and R-loops exhibited significantly up-regulated or down-regulated signals in the dhx9KO mESCs compared to the wildtype mESCs.
source: Notably, compared to the wildtype mESCs, a large amount of G4s or R-loops within co-localized G4s and R-loops exhibited significantly up-regulated or down-regulated signals in the dhx9KO mESCs (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), suggesting that Dhx9 could unwind or promote the formation of co-localized G4s and R-loops in mESCs.
evidence: Supported by HepG4-seq and HBD-seq data comparing WT and dhx9KO mESCs shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only a small proportion of co-localized G4s and R-loops displayed differential G4s and R-loops at the same time in the dhx9KO mESCs.
source: Interestingly, only a small proportion of co-localized G4s and R-loops displayed differential G4s and R-loops at the same time in the dhx9KO mESCs (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that Dhx9 cannot simultaneously unwind or promote G4s and R-loops within co-localized G4 and R-loop regions and that multiple helicases or regulators are required for modulating these regions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of differential G4s and R-loops shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Loss-of-Dhx9-induced differential co-localized G4s and R-loops preferentially localize in the active and bivalent promoters and all three types of enhancers.
source: Given that co-localized G4s and R-loops have been shown to be enriched in active promoters and enhancers (Figure 5D–F), the loss-of-Dhx9-induced differential co-localized G4s and R-loops preferentially localize in the active and bivalent promoters and all three types of enhancers (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Loss of Dhx9 resulted in 1647 significantly up-regulated genes and 1916 significantly down-regulated genes.
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 1647 significantly up-regulated genes and 1916 significantly down-regulated genes in the absence of Dhx9 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Loss of Dhx9 resulted in hundreds of G4-, R-loop-, and G4&R-loop-associated genes with significantly differential expression.

claim: Co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes that showed differential expression after knocking out Dhx9 are mainly involved in negative regulation of cell differentiation, head development, positive regulation of cell motility, DNA-binding transcription activator activity, pattern specification process, embryonic organ morphogenesis, et al.

claim: Dhx9 knockout in the mouse causes embryonic lethality.

claim: Dhx9 knockdown leads to large structural changes in chromatin and eventually cell death.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (He et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2004).

claim: 54,982 Dhx9 binding peaks were revealed in wild-type mESCs.

claim: 65.5% Dhx9 binding peaks well overlapped with 69.9% co-localized G4s and R-loops in mESCs.

evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: G-rich sequences are highly enriched in the Dhx9 binding peaks overlapping with co-localized G4s and R-loops in mESCs.

evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: 1382 significantly up-regulated peaks (823 with increased G4s and 559 with increased R-loops) and 4789 significantly down-regulated peaks (2278 with decreased G4s and 2511 with decreased R-loops) were identified in Dhx9-bound co-localized G4s and R-loops in dhx9KO mESCs.
source: We next compared the Dhx9-bound co-localized G4s and R-loops in wild-type and dhx9KO mESCs, and identified 1382 significantly up-regulated peaks (823 with increased G4s and 559 with increased R-loops) and 4789 significantly down-regulated peaks (2278 with decreased G4s and 2511 with decreased R-loops) (Figure 7F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F)

claim: Dhx9-bound differential co-localized G4s and R-loops account for ~50–75% of differential co-localized G4s and R-loops in absence of Dhx9.
source: accounting for ~50–75% of differential co-localized G4s and R-loops in absence of Dhx9 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of differential peaks bound by Dhx9 versus all differential peaks.

claim: Dhx9-bound differential co-localized G4s and R-loops are mainly localized in the active and bivalent promoters and all three types of enhancers.

claim: The Dhx9-bound differential co-localized G4s and R-loops were linked to 852 genes with significantly differential expression.

source: Several key regulators of mouse embryonic stem cell and embryonic development, such as Nanog, Lin28a, Bmp4, Wnt8a, Gata2, and Lef1, were shown to be transcriptionally regulated by Dhx9 through direct modulation of their associated G4s and R-loops (Figure 7I).

claim: Dhx9 significantly contributes to transcriptional regulation of co-localized G4s and R-loops-associated genes.

claim: The RNA levels of Lin28a and Oct4 were significantly decreased and the RNA level of Nanog was significantly increased when Dhx9 was knocked out.
source: To understand the role of Dhx9 in regulating the cell fate of mESCs, we first examined the RNA levels of several key genes that maintain the pluripotency of mESCs by quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) and found that the RNA levels of Lin28a and Oct4 were significantly decreased and the RNA level of Nanog was significantly increased when Dhx9 was knocked out (Figure 8A).

claim: dhx9KO mESCs produce obviously lower level of Lin28a protein than wild-type mESCs.

evidence: Supported by western blot data.

claim: The protein level of Nanog was significantly decreased in dhx9KO mESCs, in contrast to the RNA level.
source: whereas in contrast to the RNA level, the protein level of Nanog was significantly decreased in dhx9KO mESCs, suggesting that Dhx9 directly or indirectly modulates the translation of Nanog (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The loss of Dhx9 leads to reduced protein level of Nanog, but not Oct4.

evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Dhx9 regulates the self-renewal and differentiation capacities of mESCs.

evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing effects on proliferation, cell cycle, and differentiation.

evidence: Supported by comparison of signal intensities between methods and cell types.

source: In HEK293 cells, HBD-seq, MapR, and GST-2xHBD CUT&Tag identified 42,488, 12,520, and 17,570 peaks, respectively
